ops.new_text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common arrhythmia, and in people with asymptomatic AF the first presentation may be a stroke or heart failure \cite{Kashou_2021}. In the Framingham Heart Study, AF was associated with a near fivefold excess of stroke. The stroke risk attributable to AF rose from 1.5\% at ages 50 to 59 to 23.5\% at ages 80 to 89 \cite{Wolf_1991}. Over 50 years of the Framingham Heart Study, the age-adjusted prevalence of AF rose about fourfold and its incidence more than tripled, in part through more intensive surveillance \cite{Schnabel_2015}. Identifying the people who will develop AF could therefore guide monitoring before a first complication. Clinical risk scores such as CHARGE-AF estimate this risk from routine variables \cite{Alonso_2013}. These scores need the abstraction of clinical data, which takes time, whereas a model applied to a single ECG at the point of care needs no additional data abstraction \cite{Kashou_2021}. The resting 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is thus a candidate source of risk information in its own right.

ops.new_text: In the one-year design, the fused model had the highest AUROC of the methods compared, 0.7776 (95\% CI [0.7664, 0.7888]) (Table~\ref{tab:oneyear}). Its interval lay above the CNN's interval of [0.7226, 0.7469]. It also lay above the interval of ECG-only BTTN, 0.7397 [0.7275, 0.7517], so the fused model discriminated better than ECG-only BTTN. The fused model's interval overlapped the interval of the clinical model, 0.7597 [0.7488, 0.7713]. The study reports no paired interval for the difference between the fused and clinical models, so their estimates are reported side by side. The CNN reached 0.7350, with an interval that overlapped that of ECG-only BTTN, so the two are comparable on this cohort. ECG-only BTTN exceeded linear BTTR, at 0.5967 [0.5824, 0.6115], with intervals that do not overlap.
